title: Container Incident Response
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of container incident response.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to container incident response.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Container Incident Response. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Operations need signals that help explain what happened: application logs, health checks, runtime/resource metrics, daemon events, and a written runbook. A healthy process is not always the same as a healthy application; define checks around the behavior that matters. Learning container incident response helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Container Incident Response
items.text: Operational signals should help answer what failed, when it failed, and what changed. Establish a baseline and record the checks used to decide that the service recovered.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for container incident response. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Container Incident Response
content_blocks.code:
docker ps -a
docker logs --tail 50 CONTAINER_NAME
docker inspect CONTAINER_NAME
content_blocks.expected_output: The commands show container state, recent application output, and the inspectable runtime configuration for a chosen container.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Replace CONTAINER_NAME with a container from your disposable lab. Preserve the exact error text before changing settings.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Read-only diagnostics; no reset is required.
content_blocks.safety_note: Do not include secrets or personal data in captured logs or incident reports.

task: Apply container incident response to a small local case. Record the configuration or command, expected result, observed result, one limitation/edge case, and how you verified the result.
hints: Begin with read-only inspection commands and identify the active Docker context before any mutating action.
Use a disposable name, local test image, and synthetic data; change one thing at a time.
If the outcome differs, preserve the exact error and logs, check the official reference for your installed version, and document the verified fix.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
